summary: Blister agents that injure skin, eyes, and airway. Sulfur mustard is a delayed alkylating injury with no antidote — decontamination within the first 2 minutes is the only thing that changes outcome, and the late killer is bone-marrow suppression. Lewisite hurts immediately, causes systemic arsenic toxicity, and has an antidote (dimercaprol). Phosgene oxime causes immediate, intense pain and rapid tissue necrosis.
whyThisMatters: With mustard, the injury is set in the first minutes but does not show for hours, so a casualty who feels well is triaged low and decontaminated late — after the alkylation is already done. The management errors that follow are treating it like a thermal burn (over-resuscitating with fluid), patching the eyes (promotes adhesions), and missing the marrow nadir a week later when neutropenic sepsis is what actually kills. Lewisite is the opposite trap — immediate pain that is easy to recognize but easy to under-treat systemically.
clinicalTakeaway: Decontamination is the treatment for all three — remove clothing and use RSDL or soap and water; for mustard it must be within ~2 minutes to limit injury, but decontaminate regardless of delay to protect staff. Sulfur mustard: no antidote — supportive burn care with LESS fluid than a thermal burn of the same size, meticulous wound and ocular care (irrigate, topical antibiotic and mydriatic, petrolatum to lid margins, do NOT patch), airway management for laryngeal/tracheobronchial injury, and CBC monitoring with G-CSF and reverse isolation for the day 7-14 leukopenic nadir. Lewisite: same decon plus dimercaprol (BAL) IM for systemic toxicity or large exposure, and treat the capillary-leak "lewisite shock" with fluids. Phosgene oxime: decon, aggressive analgesia, and supportive wound/airway care — no antidote.

body.text: Sulfur and nitrogen mustard (HD / H / HT; HN)

items: Mechanism: a bifunctional alkylating agent — cross-links DNA, depletes glutathione, and triggers inflammation and apoptosis in rapidly dividing cells (basal epidermis, corneal epithelium, airway mucosa, bone marrow, GI crypts).

Onset is DELAYED: asymptomatic latent period of 2-24 h (shorter with higher dose, heat, humidity, and in moist body areas — axilla, groin, perineum). A garlic/mustard/horseradish odor may be noted at exposure.
Skin: erythema then large, dome-shaped bullae with a rim of erythema; the blister fluid is not itself vesicant. Deep partial-thickness pattern; heals slowly with dyspigmentation.

Eyes (most sensitive organ): lacrimation, blepharospasm, photophobia, conjunctivitis, corneal erosion and edema; severe exposure causes delayed corneal scarring/neovascularization and permanent visual loss.

Airway: hoarseness, cough, and a fibrinous pseudomembrane with mucosal sloughing that can obstruct proximal airways; lower-airway injury → bronchitis, ARDS, secondary bacterial pneumonia (the usual pulmonary cause of death).

Systemic: bone-marrow suppression — leukopenia beginning ~day 3, nadir ~day 7-14, with thrombocytopenia and anemia; neutropenic sepsis is the classic late killer. Also nausea/vomiting, and at high dose GI mucosal injury.

Management (no antidote): decontaminate immediately (RSDL or soap and water; the 2-minute window limits injury but decon still protects staff at any time). Burn-type care but resuscitate with LESS fluid than an equivalent thermal burn — mustard burns are less fluid-avid and over-resuscitation causes harm; titrate to urine output. Wound care as for partial-thickness burns, watch for infection. Eyes: copious irrigation, topical antibiotic, topical mydriatic/cycloplegic for comfort and to prevent synechiae, petrolatum to lid margins to prevent adhesions, and do NOT patch. Airway: humidified oxygen, bronchodilators, early intubation for laryngeal edema or pseudomembrane; bronchoscopy to clear casts. Marrow: serial CBC, G-CSF (filgrastim) for significant neutropenia, reverse isolation, transfusion support; consider stem-cell support for near-lethal exposures. Analgesia is often substantial.
An organoarsenical vesicant. Unlike mustard, it causes IMMEDIATE pain and irritation on contact (seconds to minutes) — useful for recognition and early self-decon.
Skin and eye injury resemble mustard but develop faster; grey blanched skin at contact points progresses to bullae and deeper necrosis.

Systemic arsenic toxicity from absorption: increased capillary permeability with third-spacing and hypotension ("lewisite shock"), hepatic and renal injury, and hemolysis; pulmonary edema from inhalation.

Antidote: dimercaprol (British Anti-Lewisite, BAL) IM chelates the arsenic — indicated for systemic effects, large cutaneous exposure, or significant inhalation; dimercaprol skin/eye ointments exist but are largely unavailable. Oral succimer (DMSA) or DMPS are alternatives/adjuncts for arsenic burden. Treat lewisite shock with aggressive isotonic fluids and pressors as needed.
Decontamination and supportive wound/ocular/airway care otherwise parallel mustard (but there is no significant delayed marrow suppression).
An urticant / corrosive agent (not a true blister agent — it does not form fluid-filled vesicles). Causes IMMEDIATE, severe pain on contact.
Skin: blanching with an erythematous ring within seconds, a wheal within ~30 minutes (urticaria-like), then a brown-black eschar and necrosis over days; injury can be full-thickness and slow to heal.
Eyes and airway are highly sensitive — intense irritation, lacrimation, and pulmonary edema with inhalation.

No antidote. Immediate decontamination (it penetrates fast, so decon has a very short useful window), aggressive analgesia, and supportive wound care, ocular irrigation, and airway/pulmonary support as for the other agents.

body.text: Timing tells the agent apart at the bedside: mustard is painless for hours then blisters; lewisite and phosgene oxime hurt immediately on contact. All three: decontaminate now, do not patch chemically injured eyes, and for mustard specifically, resist the reflex to give thermal-burn fluid volumes and remember the marrow nadir a week out.
